slides.page_title: Lazy Futures: Nothing Runs Until Polled

items: `async fn` returns an anonymous type implementing `Future`
Calling it runs zero user code — no body executes
A future is a value, not a task: state built, work not done
Side effects you expect at call time defer to the first poll

lines: let f = fetch(url);   // nothing happened yet
let body = f.await;   // NOW it starts

left.title: JS / Go
items: `Promise` is eager and hot
Constructed = already running
`go f()` starts immediately

right.title: Rust
items: Future is cold until polled
Needs an explicit executor
`.await` or `spawn` starts it
`Poll::Pending` = not done, will wake later
`Poll::Ready(T)` = value produced, future finished

blocks.title: Built But Never Used
items: `#[must_use]`: unused implementer of Future that must be used
Warning only — it compiles and does nothing
Dropping a future mid-flight silently cancels it
No code after the last poll ever runs
`timeout(select(a, b))` builds ONE state machine
No per-combinator allocation — zero-cost composition
`async { .. }` blocks are lazy too
`async move { .. }` takes ownership of its captures

blocks.title: Rule Of Thumb
blocks.text: A future is a recipe. The runtime is the cook. Written recipes feed nobody.

items: Compiler rewrites each `async fn` into an enum state machine
One variant per await point, plus start and done
Variants store only locals that live across an await
Locals that do not cross an await stay stack slots
Each `poll` resumes at the last await, runs to the next `Pending`

slides.page_title: The State Machine Under async fn

items: A local borrowed across an await points into the same struct
Futures are self-referential — moving them dangles pointers
`Pin<&mut T>` promises no move after the first poll
`Unpin` = safe to move anyway; most hand-written futures are
Compiler-generated futures are NOT `Unpin`

rows: max of live state, not sum

blocks.title: Recursion Needs Indirection
items: An `async fn` calling itself has infinite size
Wrap the recursive call in `Box::pin`
Or use the `async_recursion` crate
Not a syscall, not a thread yield
It is a `return Poll::Pending` from the state machine
No allocation per await — the chain is one flat struct
That flatness is the key win over GC languages

blocks.title: Read The Shape
blocks.text: Name the locals crossing each await and you can predict the future's size.

items: An await point is the only place an async fn can suspend
Between them, execution is uninterrupted
`.await` on a ready future returns instantly — no yield
Cooperative: the runtime cannot preempt you, ever
State needed after an await must live in the future
Cancellation happens only at await points
A dropped future stops between two awaits, never mid-statement
`select!` may drop the losing branch outright
A partially-read buffer in that branch is lost
`std::sync::MutexGuard` is not `Send` and blocks peers
Held across an await it stalls the whole worker
`tokio::sync::Mutex` for guards that must cross awaits
Prefer `std::sync::Mutex` for short non-await sections
Await-in-loop is strictly sequential — N round trips
`join_all` or `FuturesUnordered` for real concurrency

blocks.title: Compile Error To Know
items: await is only allowed inside async functions and blocks
Cause: `.await` written in a plain `fn`
Fix: make the fn `async`, or `block_on` at the edge

blocks.title: Between Awaits You Own The Core
blocks.text: Nothing interrupts you and nothing cancels you. Reach an await, or the core stays yours.

items: `Context` carries one thing that matters: the `Waker`
Contract: return `Pending` only after arranging a later `wake()`
`waker.wake()` queues the task; it does not run it inline

blocks.q: My future returns `Pending` and never runs again. Why?
a_bullets: It returned `Pending` without registering a waker
Nothing will ever put the task back on the ready queue
The classic lost-wakeup bug — hangs, silently, forever

items: `wake_by_ref()` avoids consuming a waker you reuse
Spurious wakeups are legal — poll must re-check its condition
So `poll` must be idempotent, never destructive
Store the newest waker each poll: tasks change threads
An old waker goes stale and wakes nobody
Leaf futures — timers, sockets — hold the wakers
Combinators just forward the `Context` down the chain

blocks.title: Waker Internals
items: `std::task::Waker` is a type-erased vtable handle
Built from `RawWaker` plus `RawWakerVTable`
`futures::task::AtomicWaker` for register-and-wake, one consumer

blocks.title: Mental Model
blocks.text: `Pending` is a promise to knock on the door later. No knock, no wake, no progress.

items: Rust ships the `Future` trait in std but NO runtime
You pick one, and it colors the whole dependency tree
Executor: owns the ready queue, calls `poll` on tasks
Reactor: owns the OS event source, wakes tasks
`block_on` drives one future to completion on this thread
It is the bridge from sync code into async code
`tokio::spawn` hands a future to the executor
Returns a `JoinHandle<T>` you can await or abort
Spawned tasks keep running after the handle drops
Task = green thread sized in bytes, not an 8 MB stack
Millions of tasks are feasible; millions of threads are not
`Builder::new_current_thread()` — no `Send` bound needed
Use `spawn_local` there for non-`Send` work
Work stealing: idle workers pull from busy workers' queues

blocks.title: Runtime Panics
items: Tokio timer or socket under another runtime: there is no reactor running
`block_on` nested inside async: Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime
One runtime per process is the norm
Pass a `Handle` instead of creating a second

blocks.title: Two Halves
blocks.text: Every runtime is a queue that polls plus an event source that wakes. Name which half misbehaves.

left.title: join! / join_all
items: One task, interleaved
N futures, one core
Fine for I/O, useless for CPU

right.title: spawn
items: Many tasks, many cores
Real parallelism
Needs `Send` and `'static`
`tokio::join!(a, b)` polls both in the current task
Returns a tuple once every branch finishes
`try_join!` short-circuits on the first `Err`
Fan out with parallelism: `spawn` each, await the handles
`tokio::select!` returns the first ready branch
It DROPS the rest — read the cancel-safety table
In a loop, use `&mut fut` or a pinned future
Otherwise each iteration restarts the branch from scratch
`FuturesUnordered` polls a live set, yields as each finishes
`join_all(v)` runs N futures in one task — I/O only
`Stream` is the async `Iterator`
`poll_next` yields `Poll<Option<T>>`
Consume: `while let Some(x) = s.next().await`

blocks.title: Three Free Idioms
items: Backpressure is free: `send().await` suspends when full
`CancellationToken` plus `select!` = graceful shutdown
`timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), fut).await` gives `Err(Elapsed)`
A future is `Send` iff every value held ACROSS an await is `Send`
Locals that die before the await never enter the question
future cannot be sent between threads safely
note: ... held across an await point
`Rc<T>` or `RefCell<T>` across an await kills `Send`
Reach for `Arc<T>` and `tokio::sync::Mutex` instead
`std::sync::MutexGuard` is `!Send` — scope it or go async
`'static` does not mean lives forever
It means borrows nothing from the caller
Fix: clone the data, or move an `Arc` into the async block
Non-`Send` work belongs on `spawn_local` inside a `LocalSet`
Or on a dedicated current-thread runtime
Auto traits leak: no `impl Future + Send` on trait methods unaided
`async fn` in traits (stable 1.75) has no `Send` bound
Use `trait_variant` or `#[async_trait]` to get one
`#[async_trait]` boxes it: one alloc, dynamic dispatch per call

blocks.title: Debug Trick
items: `fn assert_send<T: Send>(_: T) {}`
Call it on the future where it is built
The error names the offending local, not the spawn site

blocks.title: One Sentence
blocks.text: `Send` is about what survives an await. `'static` is about what you borrowed.
One Blocked Poll Kills A Thread

items: A blocked `poll` occupies its worker thread entirely
No other task on that thread can run, at all
Tokio multi-thread defaults to one worker per core
N blocking calls stall N cores

blocks.title: Symptoms
items: Latency spikes with no CPU explanation
Timers firing late, heartbeats missed
Throughput cliff under load
`std::thread::sleep`, `std::fs`, `reqwest::blocking`
Synchronous DB drivers, contended `Mutex`
Heavy CPU too: parsing 200 MB JSON, image resize
Hashing a password blocks with no syscall in sight

slides.page_title: Blocking Inside Async: The Cardinal Sin

items: `tokio-console` shows per-task poll times and stalls
Or `--cfg tokio_unstable` poll-time histogram metrics
Rule: any poll past 10-100 microseconds gets split or moved
Async file I/O is a lie on Linux
`tokio::fs` is `spawn_blocking` under the hood
`argon2` at 100 ms destroys a 4-core runtime at 40 req/s

blocks.title: Why It Is A Sin
blocks.text: You are not borrowing a thread from a pool. You are freezing the only thread that can make progress.

left.title: Async wins
items: I/O-bound, 10k+ sockets
Proxies, chat, scrapers
High concurrency

right.title: Threads win
items: CPU-bound work
Low connection counts
Simple blocking scripts
An await adds a poll and a possible queue hop
A hot path with no I/O is faster written sync
Compile time: deep nesting makes huge monomorphized types
Builds get slow and stay slow
Stack traces show executor frames, not your logical chain
Async infects its callers all the way up
A sync trait cannot call async code without `block_on`
A crate must pick tokio vs smol vs async-std traits
`AsyncRead` differs between futures-rs and tokio
In libraries stay runtime-agnostic, or feature-gate it

blocks.title: Do Not Go Async
items: A CLI making three HTTP calls
`ureq` plus threads is simpler and faster to write
You finish before the runtime finishes compiling

blocks.title: Pick By Workload
blocks.text: Count sockets, not opinions. Below a few hundred connections, threads are the cheaper answer.

slides.page_title: Common Mistakes And The Full Picture

items: Forgetting `.await` — the future is built, then dropped
Nothing happens; you get only a `must_use` warning
Awaiting inside a loop when you meant concurrency
N sequential round trips instead of one wave

lines: for u in urls { get(u).await; } // N trips

items: Holding a `std::sync` lock across an await
Result: a `!Send` error, or a quietly stalled worker
Blocking on the runtime thread
The number one production incident in async Rust
Unbounded `mpsc`, or unbounded `spawn` in a loop
Memory grows until the OOM killer decides for you
Ignoring `select!` cancel safety
Silently dropped reads and half-finished writes
Spawning and never awaiting the `JoinHandle`
Panics inside that task are swallowed whole
`spawn` queues — the task may not start before your next await
Detached tasks outliving shutdown: use `JoinSet` or `TaskTracker`

rows: Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime
future cannot be sent between threads safely

items: `tokio-console` for live task state and poll times
`RUST_BACKTRACE` plus `#[track_caller]` for real origins
`tracing` spans that survive across awaits

blocks.title: The Whole Handbook, One Line
blocks.text: Futures do nothing until a runtime polls them, they suspend only at awaits, wakers bring them back, and blocking one poll stops everything.

caption.text: Your Rust future did nothing when you called it. That is not a bug — it is the entire design. Ten pages on lazy futures, the state machine under async fn, wakers, runtimes, Send bounds, and the one sin that takes production down: blocking a poll.
